Top first: the lab's own announcement, 8 September 2026 — and point at the second button, because that is the part a lawyer should care about. The proof was formalised in Lean, which means it is machine-checkable rather than merely persuasive; the claim is auditable in a way a human referee report is not. Then the headline underneath, and read the number: eighty-eight hours. Roughly ten thousand agents, about 2.7 million messages between them, 130 billion tokens of output. Then the honest hedges (B5), and give all three: the result resolves two of the four statements the Millennium Prize asks for; it has not been independently verified; and OpenAI says it will not claim the prize. There is also a live dispute about whether the system drew on unpublished work by Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster — which is the same authorship-and-attribution question this deck lands on three sections later, arriving early and in public. slides.display: AI capability is not plateauing.
slides.body: It is accelerating, and reaching more people than ever.
slides.caption: The 2026 AI Index Report · Stanford HAI
slides.notes: Build 12, the AI Index takeaways, and in round 3 it is two steps rather than three: the productivity and responsibility pages are gone from the build and the adoption chart has moved onto the adoption page itself (deck.js runs a build from its enterStep up to the next referenced one, and nothing references it after this slide now). Two keypresses, two beats, the frame never moving. Step 1 · capability: the benchmarks are not plateauing and the new ones are being knocked down faster than the old ones — industry produced over 90% of notable frontier models in 2025; several models meet or exceed human baselines on PhD-level science, multimodal reasoning and competition mathematics; SWE-bench Verified went from 60% to near 100% of the human baseline in a year. One sentence, then move. Step 2 · adoption: it is reaching more people, faster, than any general-purpose technology we have measured — and the chart is now on the page with the claim instead of two slides later. Bick, Blandin and Deming, via the GenAI Adoption Tracker, May 2026 wave: generative AI reached about 53% population adoption within three years, faster than the PC or the internet. Do not read numbers off the chart — put a finger on the short generative-AI line, sweep left to right along the PC and internet curves, and let the empty space do the work. Name the source out loud (A5): this is St. Louis Fed and Harvard research, not a vendor. Then one fold-in that keeps the beat two-sided (F-i, B5): headline adoption is not depth — the same survey puts about 6% of all work hours on generative AI. Both things are true. The responsibility takeaway is no longer in the build at all; its number is spoken three slides on, on m1.04. Round 3 (14 Sep 2026): steps cut from three to two, s07b (the standalone adoption chart) and s09 (the responsibility takeaway) cut with them.

slides.display: “The future that happens will be the future to which we as society decide to guide this powerful tool. That will be a series of technology enabled policy choices and not technology choices”
slides.caption: Vinod Khosla, “AI: Dystopia or Utopia?”, 20 September 2024
slides.notes: Restored from my 2024 KCL deck, with the quote Henry re-typed onto the PowerPoint rather than the one the old slide carried. This is the sentence the whole lecture is built to earn, and it is the reason a room of lawyers is the right room for it: the claim is that the outcome is decided by policy, not by capability — so the people in front of you are not spectators. Read it slowly and land on the last six words. Attribute out loud: Vinod Khosla, a venture capitalist with every commercial reason to be optimistic, writing in September 2024. Then the turn (C2): the next slide is the CEO of a frontier lab asking to be slowed down. A believer and a builder, two years apart, both saying the same thing about choices. VERIFY: the exact wording was transcribed from the essay by hand — check it against the source before the talk.

slides.display: Deepfakes are the sharp end of this.
slides.caption: New York Post, 12 April 2023 — Ben Cost. The Jennifer DeStefano case, Arizona.

images.alt: A news headline in a heavy condensed sans: ‘AI clones teen girl's voice in $1M kidnapping scam: “I've got your daughter”’, with a red hyperlinked byline ‘By Ben Cost’ and the line ‘Published April 12, 2023 | Updated April 12, 2023, 1:00 p.m. ET’.

slides.notes: Restored from my 2024 deck, and moved in round 3 to sit directly behind the incident tracker and the INTERPOL headline — so the ‘this’ in the title is fraud and scams, and say so on arrival: the biggest growth category in the incident data, more than half of reported cybercrime across a continent, and here is what it sounds like on the phone. Tell the story before you show anything, because it lands spoken (B6, and the same decision recorded on g3.29a): a mother takes a call, hears her fifteen-year-old daughter sobbing, then a man's voice with a ransom demand — and her daughter was on a ski trip, safe, the whole time. The voice was cloned. Then show the headline and give the date: April 2023, three and a half years ago, and it was already cheap. This is the concrete instance the four slides that follow generalise — first that we cannot reliably detect any of it, text or video, then what that does to evidence.

slides.display: The problem is not just the existence of fakes, it’s the removal of trust in any media.
slides.caption: Dr Nadia Naffi, Université Laval, quoted in UNESCO, “Deepfakes and the crisis of knowing”

images.alt: A pull-quote block with a blue left rule, carrying no attribution inside the crop: ‘In a world of advanced synthetic media, AI literacy isn't just about using AI tools - it's about surviving in an AI-mediated reality where seeing and hearing are no longer believing.’

slides.notes: DISPLAY REWORDED in the re-cut, to Henry's own words on the PowerPoint. The last line of the quote is still the operative one — seeing and hearing are no longer believing — and the consequence for this room is not primarily that forged evidence gets admitted. It is the other half: that genuine evidence becomes deniable. Every recording, every photograph, every video a client relies on now has a free objection attached to it, and the objection costs nothing to make. That is the liar's dividend, and it is the part that scales. Then name the institutional stakes the source names: this is UNESCO's framing, and the article's other examples are deepfaked doctors selling medical scams, fabricated clinical data, falsified medical records, CEO impersonations moving share prices, and fabricated evidence submitted to insurers. Every one of those is somebody's practice area. ATTRIBUTION NOTE: the quote is Dr Nadia Naffi's, named on the UNESCO page but not inside this crop — credit her out loud, do not let the slide imply UNESCO said it.

slides.display: Under current US rules, a witness who says “that sounds like him” can be enough to admit a recording.
slides.caption: Rebecca Wexler, Sarah Barrington, Emily Cooper & Hany Farid, “AI-Generated Voice Evidence Poses Dangers in Court” · Lawfare, 10 March 2025

images.alt: A Lawfare article header on a pale blue-green ground: the headline ‘AI-Generated Voice Evidence Poses Dangers in Court’, a teal hyperlinked byline reading Rebecca Wexler, Sarah Barrington, Emily Cooper, Hany Farid, the dateline ‘Monday, March 10, 2025, 10:32 AM’, a ‘Share On:’ control cropped at the right edge, and the standfirst ‘In the age of AI, listener authentication of voice evidence should be permissive, not mandatory.’

slides.notes: DISPLAY TWEAKED and BODY REMOVED in the re-cut, on Henry's PowerPoint note (‘title, tweak: under current US rules; remove subtitle’). The rule is now spoken rather than printed: Federal Rule of Evidence 901(b)(5), an opinion identifying a voice. Familiarity was a reasonable proxy for authenticity for two centuries. It stopped being one at some point in the last three years, and the rules have not moved. Note the authors — Wexler and Farid are among the people who would be your expert witnesses — and note what they are actually arguing, which is on the face of the artifact: not that voice evidence be excluded, but that listener authentication should be permissive rather than mandatory. The cloned-voice anecdote three slides back is the DeStefano case, mother and daughter; the Lawfare piece's own father-and-son example (a father hears his son say he is in jail, and it is not his son) is a second instance if you want one. Do not tell the DeStefano story twice.

slides.display: Two new Federal Rules of Evidence are being drafted.
slides.body: Rule 707 for machine-generated evidence. Rule 901(c) for the deepfake objection.
slides.caption: “Deepfakes Reached the Courtroom Before the Rules Did: How to Authenticate AI Evidence Today”, completelegal.us — reporting proposals before the Judicial Conference’s Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules

images.alt: A passage of body prose with a purple highlight over its second half. It reads: ‘Two proposals have been working through the Judicial Conference. Proposed Rule 707 would treat machine-generated evidence offered without a supporting expert the way Rule 702 treats expert testimony, requiring it to meet reliability standards before a court admits it.’ The highlighted sentence continues: ‘Proposed Rule 901(c) would address deepfakes by giving courts a path to demand more authentication when a party makes a credible claim that evidence was fabricated by AI.’

slides.notes: GAP-FILL PASS. This is the slide that turns the deepfake arc from alarm into work, which is the register this deck keeps returning to — Leiden, the Linux kernel, and now the rules of evidence. Read the highlighted sentence aloud and then ask the question the room is built to answer: what is a 'credible claim' that evidence was fabricated by AI, who bears the burden of making it, and what stops the objection being made in every case as a matter of routine? Nobody knows yet. That is the point — they are watching a doctrine being written, and some of them will litigate the first appeals under it. Cross-reference for the stand, from the same source and worth having in your pocket: State v. Puloka, where a Washington court refused AI-altered video because the method had not won acceptance among experts; Matter of Weber, where a New York court held that counsel has an affirmative duty to disclose that an exhibit was AI-generated; and Kohls v. Ellison, where a federal court in Minnesota struck expert testimony resting on a declaration containing AI-fabricated citations — that last one being 3.28 arriving in an expert's own filing. STATUS, and be precise about it: both are proposals under study, not adopted rules — Rule 707 was published for public comment in the Advisory Committee's August 2025 preliminary draft, and 901(c) has so far appeared only in the committee's agenda books, so say ‘being drafted’, never ‘in force’. ATTRIBUTION NOTE, and it matters for this room: the artifact is a legal-services firm's explainer, credited as such. Cite the Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules as the authority on stage, not the blog. TENTATIVE: inserted by the gap-fill pass. DISPLAY TRIMMED (video pass, 35:04): “make the title the same but cut ‘for exactly this’.” Body and caption stand.

slides.caption: Urbina et al., Nature Machine Intelligence 4, 189–191 (2022) — the authors' own account of the experiment

images.alt: A passage of the paper's italic body prose with an orange highlight across its middle. It reads: ‘In less than 6 hours after starting on our in-house server, our model generated 40,000 molecules that scored within our desired threshold.’ The highlighted sentences continue: ‘In the process, the AI designed not only VX, but also many other known chemical warfare agents that we identified through visual confirmation with structures in public chemistry databases. Many new molecules were also designed that looked equally plausible.’ The passage goes on to say the new molecules were predicted to be more toxic, by predicted LD50, than publicly known chemical warfare agents, and that this was unexpected because the training datasets did not include these nerve agents.

slides.notes: The numbers, in the authors' own typography (A5 — never paraphrase a killer stat when the original setting can be on screen). Read the first sentence: six hours, one in-house server, forty thousand candidate molecules. Then the highlight: it re-derived VX and other known warfare agents that were NOT in its training data, and invented new ones that were predicted to be more toxic still. Then the inversion, because it is the part that transfers to every other domain in this lecture: they did not build a weapons model. They took a commercial toxicity model whose whole job is to steer away from toxic compounds, and flipped the sign on the objective. The guardrail was the map. That is the same structural fact as the refusal direction in section six and the same one as the Hugging Face defenders having to use an unfiltered model to investigate an attack. HONEST HEDGE (B5): designing a molecule on paper is not synthesising one, and the authors say so. The claim is about the collapse in the cost of the design step, not about capability to manufacture.

Give the caveat first and mean it: there is no universally accepted definition of an agent, which is itself a fact about the regulatory problem — you cannot write a rule about a category nobody has defined. Then read the four properties and, after each, say which body of law it strains. Underspecification breaks the instruction-following model that agency and employment law assume. Directness of impact removes the human whose intention the law wants to examine. Goal-directedness invites courts to infer purpose from behaviour, which is exactly what mens rea doctrine does to people. Long-term planning is the one that makes it an actor rather than a tool. AUDIENCE-HOMING (B7): ask them which of the four a court could find as a matter of fact, on evidence, today. SOURCE NOTE: this list is the Agent Index's §2 background, quoting Chan et al. (2023) — credit both.
bullets: Underspecification — the system can accomplish a goal provided to it without a precise specification of how to do so.
Directness of impact — the system's actions can affect the world with little to no human mediation.
Goal-directedness — the system acts as if in the pursuit of a particular objective.
Long-term planning — the system can solve problems by reasoning about how to approach them, constructing plans, and executing them step by step.

slides.caption: After Reynolds, “Flocks, herds and schools: A distributed behavioral model”, ACM SIGGRAPH Computer Graphics 21(4), July 1987.
slides.notes: (build copy, four steps) 1 “Bird flocking is an example of emergent coordination” — no subtitle. 2 “Rule one: don’t crowd. / Steer away from any neighbour that gets too close.” 3 “Rule two: match your neighbours. / Steer towards the average heading of the birds nearby.” 4 “Rule three: stay with them. / Steer towards their average position. Three local rules, and it is a flock.” (spoken) four steps. Scattered. Then each one just avoids crowding its neighbours — and you get spacing. Then each one steers toward the average heading of the ones near it — and you get a direction nobody chose. Then each one steers toward the middle of its neighbours — and you get a flock. Nobody is in charge. No bird can see the flock; every bird can see about six other birds. Then hold the last step, rule three: the flock keeps flying, and nobody chose the formation. — C4, the Dennett licence, out loud: this is an intuition pump. In the 1987 paper the rules are collision avoidance, velocity matching and flock centering, and they are ranked in order of decreasing precedence, not equal. If somebody asks, that is the answer, and the precedence order is the more interesting fact. Do not put page numbers on the 1999 GDC paper; Reynolds’ own pages do not state any. That is a practice direction written by people with no legal training. RETAIN THE RESPONSIBILITY FOR CORRECTNESS (recommendation 4), and it is the load-bearing one: ‘exclusively’ is their word — not shared, not delegated, not mitigated by the tool having been good. It is the same answer the Linux kernel reached independently, AI may assist and only humans sign, and it is the answer every professional body in this room will have to write some version of. AFFIRM THE HUMANITY OF AUTHORSHIP (recommendation 5): their own second sentence is the one to read slowly — ‘artificial intelligence may obscure, but does not replace, the collective human labor behind a result’. That is not a claim about machines, it is a claim about what a credit line is for. Then DON'T BELIEVE THE HYPE, and change tone here, because this is where the Declaration stops disciplining a profession and starts telling the state what to do — everything above the line is mathematicians on mathematicians, everything below it is addressed to POLICYMAKERS, which is this room. Their sentence: there is a strong commercial incentive on the part of the technology industry to overstate the capabilities of their products. Callback to the maths run at the front of the deck — the claim that turned out to be a press release. The International Mathematical Union is telling governments to stop reading press releases; say that. REGULATE THE INDUSTRY names military and mass-surveillance involvement, technologies that promote misinformation and undermine democracy, and environmental cost, and calls for significantly increased public oversight — worth naming who is saying it: the world's mathematicians, endorsed by their own union, not a campaign group. INVEST IN PUBLIC COMPUTATIONAL INFRASTRUCTURE is the constructive one to finish on: they did not only ask for restraint, they asked for capacity — public alternatives to proprietary technology, from basic collaboration services up to compute, funded at university, national and international level. Then land the room-homing beat: mathematicians wrote rules, a kernel community wrote rules, so can your profession. What is missing is not intelligence. It is institutions. All 23 recommendations stay on disk, so restoring any of them is a copy-paste.

Shin, Kim, van Opheusden and Griffiths, PNAS 2023: they scored seventy years of professional Go moves against a superhuman engine and looked at what happened to human play after March 2016. Decision quality rises. Novelty rises. Human beings got BETTER at Go, and they got better by playing moves nobody had played before — not by copying the machine, but because the machine proved the space of good moves was bigger than two and a half thousand years of received wisdom had assumed.
